turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I think you mean to apologize for the past, but I see no sincerity in your words, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Bennet, that you would refuse my offer based on a misinterpretation of my character.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by empty professions of love when you have consistently shown me your true nature through your words and actions, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished that you would so callously dismiss my avowals, Elizabeth, when I have been so frank with you about my feelings. Your rejection, I confess, is not unexpected, given your previous...disdain for me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your frankness is matched only by your arrogance, Mr. Darcy. I will not be swayed by your protestations of love, nor will I be insulted by your implication that my feelings towards you are somehow my fault.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I am astonished by the vehemence of your rejection. Your own feelings towards me, I had hoped, would have been tempered by the knowledge of my affection, and the efforts I have made to redeem myself in your eyes.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not astonished, Mr. Darcy. I am merely appalled that you could so callously disregard the hurt you have caused me in the past and expect me to forgive you simply because you have declared your love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You wound me, Miss Elizabeth, by implying that my declarations of love are insincere. I assure you, my feelings for you are genuine, and I expect you to acknowledge them.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You expect me to acknowledge your feelings? After everything you've done to humiliate and belittle me, I'm supposed to simply accept your declarations of love without question?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Elizabeth, that you would so callously dismiss my avowals of affection, given that I have, in fact, acted to defend your good name and reputation from the slurs of the infamous George Wickham.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may have defended my good name, Mr. Darcy, but that does not excuse your earlier behavior towards me and my family. Your interference in our affairs was unwelcome, to say the least.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I think you've made it quite clear, Mr. Darcy, that you prioritize your own interests over the well-being and dignity of those around you, and I'm afraid your sudden declaration of love only serves to highlight the vast gulf between us.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I am perplexed by your refusal of my affections, considering the numerous occasions on which I have demonstrated my admiration for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your professions of admiration mean little to me, Mr. Darcy, when I recall the way you treated my sister and the condescending manner in which you spoke to me at Netherfield.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I am perplexed by your continued obstinacy in rejecting my affections, despite the fact that I have attempted to atone for any past transgressions and have shown you every consideration.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not 'perplexed' by your affections, Mr. Darcy, but by your audacity in expecting me to forget your past behavior and accept your apologies without condition.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I expected more delicacy from you, Elizabeth. Your words, though sharp, only serve to remind me of the many occasions on which you have shown a want of appreciation for the kindnesses I have offered you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am shocked that you still do not comprehend the gravity of your past actions, Mr. Darcy. Your words of love now are nothing but a feeble attempt to salvage your damaged reputation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your sentiments are as baseless as they are unjust, Miss Bennet. I am astonished that you can so readily forget the many kindnesses I have shown you, and the sacrifices I have made for your family's benefit.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must confess, Mr. Darcy, that I find it quite remarkable you should think me so easily swayed by your words, after all the ways you have made me feel belittled and disrespected in the past. Your past behavior towards me has been nothing short of arrogant and dismissive, and I will not be won over by a few flowery phrases now.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
